title: Free grace for all
hookLine: Arminius and Wesley stressed grace that goes before, freeing everyone to respond

lines: THE GOD OF MY MERCY SHALL PREVENT ME.
cards: "The God of my mercy shall prevent me." That's a psalm, in the King James Bible, and to a modern ear it sounds alarming. Prevent me?
Stop me? But in the English of that Bible, to prevent could mean to come before, to go ahead of. The psalm is saying God's mercy will go out in front.
Keep that old meaning in your pocket. John Wesley, the Methodist leader, liked to call one of his teachings preventing grace. Today it usually goes by a longer, Latin-flavored name: prevenient grace.

teach.b: Prevenient grace: grace that comes before. Yesterday the Reformed said God chooses first, and salvation rests on that choosing.

Jacob Arminius, a Dutch teacher, and later John Wesley in England, agreed on the first part: grace must come first. Nobody climbs to God by their own strength; Augustine was right about that, they said.
But they read the Bible's wide words widely.

teach.h: THE TRUE LIGHT, FOR EVERY MAN.
teach.b: John's Gospel calls Christ "the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world."

teach.h: GRACE FREES THE WILL TO ANSWER.
teach.b: Titus says: "the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men." And Jesus says, in John: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me."
So, they taught, God's grace goes ahead of everyone, not only some. It wakes the conscience. It loosens the bent will just enough that a person can say yes to God, or turn away.
Wesley spoke of it as the first faint wish to please God, the first dawn of light. The yes still matters, but even the yes is a gift.
Methodists and other Wesleyan and Holiness churches stand in this line, and so do some Pentecostals.

The Reformed reply that it gives too much weight to the human choice; Wesleyans reply that love leaves room for a real answer, yes or no. Both sides quote scripture, both say grace first, and both pray.

teach.h: WE LOVE HIM, BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.
teach.b: The first letter of John has a line both could sign: "We love him, because he first loved us." The disagreement is over what happens next.

how: Methodist and other Wesleyan churches teach prevenient grace, God's grace going before every person and enabling them to respond, and their hymns and preaching often invite people to answer that grace.

o: grace that stops people from doing wrong
grace that goes before anyone chooses God
grace given only after a person repents

games.q: free grace for all — tap the pairs.
p: the true Light, which lighteth every man

s: in the King James psalm, prevent means stop
in that English it could mean to go before: God's mercy goes out in front.
Wesley taught that people reach God by their own strength
he taught that grace comes first and frees the will to answer. even the yes is a gift.
Wesleyans and the Reformed both say grace comes first
they differ over what happens next: whether everyone is freed to answer.

games.q: you're John Wesley. you agree with Augustine that grace must come first. but John's Gospel says the light lighteth every man. what do you teach?
o: grace comes only to a chosen few.
grace goes before everyone, freeing each person to answer.
nobody needs grace to answer God.
games.why: Wesley taught preventing grace: God's grace goes ahead of everyone, waking the conscience and freeing the will to say yes, or to turn away.

practice: Listen inward for a small nudge of good you've been stepping around, an apology, a call to an old friend, without inventing one, and let it grow clear. Then choose one small step that would answer it.
If you pray, give thanks for the nudge itself; if you don't, notice that it came before you chose to listen.

wordCard.voice: Prevenient grace. Grace that goes before anyone chooses, reaching everyone and freeing them to answer. Arminius and Wesley stressed it.

carryVoice: Your line: grace goes before. Even the yes, in this teaching, is a gift. See you tomorrow.
